hfaqs.a: No. Start with spoken Malayalam in Roman letters, and let the script come second. Learners who speak first stay motivated far longer than learners who drill letters for a month before saying a word.
hfaqs.q: Must I learn the Malayalam script before speaking?

hfaqs.a: നമസ്കാരം for respect, അതെ and ഇല്ല, നന്ദി, ദയവായി, ശരി, and ഞാൻ — I. With those seven you can open any interaction in Kerala politely while your vocabulary grows underneath.
hfaqs.q: Which words should I learn in week one?

hfaqs.a: The famous ഴ plus retroflexes — ള, ണ, long-short vowel pairs. Ten minutes of daily listening retunes your ears within weeks; the pronunciation page walks you through each one.

topics.desc: നമസ്കാരം opens every door in Kerala — plus mornings, welcomes and warm goodbyes. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Yes, and nobody will mind — നമസ്കാരം with folded hands is understood and loved everywhere Malayalam is spoken. With close friends a smile and സുഖമാണോ? (are you well?) feels warmer.
faqs.q: Can I just say namaskaram everywhere?

faqs.a: നമസ്കാരം with folded hands and a small nod, and നിങ്ങൾ (ningal — formal you) until invited closer. Add ചേട്ടൻ (chettan) or ചേച്ചി (chechi) for someone slightly older — it warms everything instantly.
faqs.q: How do I greet an elder respectfully?

faqs.a: വീണ്ടും കാണാം (veendum kaanaam — we'll meet again) is the warm standard. പോയിട്ട് വരാം (poyitt varaam — I'll go and come back) is the classic respectful farewell — receive it with a smile and a nod.
faqs.q: How do Malayalis say goodbye?

topics.note: A note on സുഖമാണോ vs സുഖമല്ലേ. സുഖമാണോ? (sughamaano) is the everyday are you well? — warm, quick, everywhere. സുഖമല്ലേ? is its cosy confirmation-style twin, heard among friends. Start with സുഖമാണോ; the rest arrives with ammamas.
paras: നമസ്കാരം (namaskaram) is the one greeting that never fails. Folded hands, a small nod, and it works with strangers, elders, shopkeepers and officials — exactly the people a learner meets first. Say it clearly, hold the folded hands half a second, and Kerala opens to you.

Mornings get their own greeting: സുപ്രഭാതം (suprabhaatam — good morning), heard in offices, schools and chayakadas until about eleven. Evenings soften to ശുഭസായാഹ്നം (shubhasaayaahnam). Time-stamped greetings signal that you live in the language, not just visit it.

Welcomes are grand in Malayali culture: സ്വാഗതം (svaagatam — welcome) opens homes, shops and hearts. Guests are greeted standing, often with water or chaya before a single question. Return the warmth — വന്നു, നന്ദി (I've come, thank you) — and you are family within minutes.

Goodbyes promise return, never end: വീണ്ടും കാണാം (we'll meet again) is the everyday farewell; സൂക്ഷിക്കണം (sookshikkanam — take care) adds affection. Leave every conversation with a നമസ്കാരം and a smile — in Kerala, how you leave is remembered longer than how you came.

topics.desc: Vowels, consonants, conjuncts and the famous ഴ — the Malayalam alphabet without tears. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Fifteen vowels (സ്വരങ്ങൾ) and thirty-six consonants (വ്യഞ്ജനങ്ങൾ) — 51+ letters that combine into conjuncts. Sounds huge, behaves simply: learn the shapes and the combinations assemble themselves.
faqs.q: How many letters does Malayalam have?

faqs.a: ഴ (zha) — the retroflex approximant Malayalam shares with Tamil: പഴം, വാഴ. Curl the tongue back without touching, voice it. Listen, curl, practise: it arrives within weeks.
faqs.q: What is the hardest Malayalam letter?

faqs.a: Yes — in writing: ഖ ഘ ഛ ഝ ഠ ഢ ഥ ധ ഫ ഭ appear in Sanskrit loans (ക്ഷമ, ധർമ്മം). Daily Malayalam softens most of them; recognise them in print, relax in speech.
faqs.q: Does Malayalam have kh, gh, bh sounds?

topics.note: A note on ചന്ദ്രക്കല (chandrakkala). The little crescent ് kills a consonant's hidden vowel: ക is ka, ക് is just k. Malayalam writes pure consonants with the chandrakkala and syllables without — ക് + അ = ക. One crescent, and the whole reading system clicks.
paras: Malayalam vowels (സ്വരങ്ങൾ) come in fifteen: അ ആ ഇ ഈ ഉ ഊ ഋ എ ഏ ഐ ഒ ഓ ഔ അം അഃ. Short and long pairs — അ/ആ, ഇ/ഈ, ഉ/ഊ — change meaning completely: കല (kala — art) versus കാലം (kaalam — time). Length is meaning in Malayalam; stretch with care.

Consonants (വ്യഞ്ജനങ്ങൾ) run five rows deep: ക ഖ ഗ ഘ ങ, ച ഛ ജ ഝ ഞ, ട ഠ ഡ ഢ ണ, ത ഥ ദ ധ ന, പ ഫ ബ ഭ മ — plus യ ര ല വ ശ ഷ സ ഹ ള ഴ റ. Round, curly, generous — the script that writes Tamil's sister with Sanskrit's wardrobe.

Vowels and consonants marry into കൂട്ടക്ഷരങ്ങൾ (koottaksharams): ക് + അ = ക (ka), ക് + ആ = കാ (kaa). Learn the vowel-signs once and every consonant sings the same song — the system is vast but perfectly regular.

Then the crown jewel: ഴ (zha), the retroflex approximant — പഴം (fruit), വാഴ (plantain). Curl the tongue back without touching the roof, voice it, and feel the most Malayali sound in existence. Natives will grin when you land it; the grin is worth weeks of practice.

topics.desc: ഒന്ന് രണ്ട് മൂന്ന് to നൂറ് — plus clock time and market-ready counting. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: International digits for daily life — prices, phones, buses all use them. Malayalam has traditional number words in full use (ഒന്ന്, പത്ത്, നൂറ്) but modern digits in print.
faqs.q: Malayalam digits or international digits?

faqs.a: Take the number, add മണി (mani — hour): മൂന്ന് മണി (three o'clock). Half past adds -അര: മൂന്നര is half past three. One rule, every clock in Kerala.
faqs.q: How do I say the time in Malayalam?

faqs.a: എത്ര? (ethra — how much?). Then listen for the number plus രൂപ (roopa — rupees). Market Malayalam is the fastest teacher there is.
faqs.q: How do I ask the price?

topics.note: A note on ഒന്നര, രണ്ടര. Half hours glue -അര to the number: ഒന്നര (1:30), മൂന്നര (3:30), അഞ്ചര (5:30). Every language hides one clock trick; Malayalam's is അര. Learn it and sound native instantly.
paras: One to ten: ഒന്ന് (onn), രണ്ട് (rand), മൂന്ന് (moonn), നാല് (naal), അഞ്ച് (anch), ആറ് (aar), ഏഴ് (ezh), എട്ട് (ett), ഒമ്പത് (ombath), പത്ത് (pathth). Chant them in rhythm — Malayalam numbers love rhythm — and they stick in days, not weeks.

Eleven to nineteen build on പത്ത്: പതിനൊന്ന് (11), പന്ത്രണ്ട് (12), പതിമൂന്ന് (13)... then the tens march: ഇരുപത് (20), മുപ്പത് (30), നാല്പത് (40), അമ്പത് (50), അറുപത് (60), എഴുപത് (70), എൺപത് (80), തൊണ്ണൂറ് (90), നൂറ് (100). Past twenty, glue tens to units — ഇരുപത്തൊന്ന് (21) — and count to a thousand (ആയിരം) without fear.

Money runs on numbers: the currency is the രൂപ (roopa — rupee), and എത്ര? (ethra — how much?) is the most useful sentence in Kerala. Listen for the number, repeat it back — അമ്പത്? (fifty?) — and your first Malayalam transaction completes itself.

Time reuses numbers with മണി (mani — hour): രണ്ട് മണി (two o'clock), അഞ്ച് മണി (five o'clock). ഇപ്പോൾ സമയം എത്ര? (what time is it now?) is the question; half hours add -അര. Numbers, money, clocks: one skill, three daily victories.

topics.desc: Names, homes and small talk — your first real Malayalam conversations, line by line. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: നിങ്ങളുടെ പേര് എന്താണ്? (ningalude perenthaan — what is your name?) for respect; നിന്റെ പേര് എന്താണ്? (ninte perenthaan) for friends and children. Answer with എന്റെ പേര്... (ente per — my name is...). Names first, always.
faqs.q: How do I ask someone's name?

faqs.a: നിങ്ങൾ എവിടെ നിന്ന് വരുന്നു? (where are you from?) — then answer for yourself: ഞാൻ ... നിന്ന് വരുന്നു. Origin questions are the universal second question; prepare your answer before you need it.
faqs.q: How do I say where I'm from?

faqs.a: പതുക്കെ സംസാരിക്കൂ (please speak slowly) and വീണ്ടും പറയൂ (please say it again). Said with a smile, these two sentences make every Malayali slow down and help.
faqs.q: What do I say when people speak too fast?

topics.note: A note on നിങ്ങൾ, നീ and താൻ. Malayalam has two yous where English has one: നിങ്ങൾ (ningal — formal/plural) and നീ (nee — familiar). Start with നിങ്ങൾ for every adult; let friendship invite you to നീ.
paras: Every first conversation follows the same dance: നമസ്കാരം, നിങ്ങളുടെ പേര് എന്താണ്? (what is your name?), എന്റെ പേര്... (my name is...), നിങ്ങൾ എവിടെ നിന്ന് വരുന്നു? (where are you from?). Four lines, and you have had a real conversation. Practise them in order until they flow without thinking.

Small talk runs on three questions: നിങ്ങൾ എന്ത് ചെയ്യുന്നു? (what do you do?), മലയാളം സംസാരിക്കുമോ? (do you speak Malayalam?), ഭക്ഷണം കഴിച്ചോ? (have you eaten? — asked with genuine care). Answer briefly, ask back immediately — നിങ്ങൾ? — because conversations are volleys, not speeches.

When the torrent comes — and Malayali hospitality pours words — deploy the brakes: പതുക്കെ സംസാരിക്കൂ (please speak slowly), എനിക്ക് മനസ്സിലായില്ല (I didn't understand), വീണ്ടും പറയൂ (please say it again). Every Malayali honours these instantly; they are the learner's seatbelt.

Close warmly and promise return: നിങ്ങളെ കണ്ടതിൽ സന്തോഷം (pleased to meet you), വീണ്ടും കാണാം (we'll meet again). Leave with a നമസ്കാരം and the door stays open — Malayalam conversations end the way they begin: with folded hands.

topics.desc: പോകുക, വരിക, കഴിക്കുക — the twelve verbs that run daily life, plus how they bend. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Malayalam verbs are cited in -ഉക form: പോകുക (to go), വരിക (to come). Polite commands end in -ൂ: പോകൂ (please go), വരൂ (please come). Learn citation forms first, politeness second.
faqs.q: Why do verbs end in -ഉക?

faqs.a: ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (I go), നീ പോകുന്നു (you go), അവൻ പോകുന്നു (he goes) — same form! Malayalam verbs don't change by person, only by tense. The easiest verb system in India.
faqs.q: How do Malayalam verbs change?

faqs.a: ഇല്ല (illa — no/not) negates everything simply: അറിയില്ല (don't know), വേണ്ട (don't want). One negator, endless uses — Malayalam keeps no simple.
faqs.q: How do I say no to a verb?

topics.note: A note on വരൂ vs വാ. വാ (vaa) calls a friend to come; വരൂ (varoo) welcomes a guest like royalty. Same verb, different universe — the -ൂ ending is pure respect. When in doubt, add the respect: Malayalis forgive stiff politeness instantly and casual rudeness never.
paras: Twelve verbs carry daily life: പോകുക (go), വരിക (come), കഴിക്കുക (eat), കുടിക്കുക (drink), വായിക്കുക (read), എഴുതുക (write), ചെയ്യുക (do), സംസാരിക്കുക (speak), കൊടുക്കുക (give), എടുക്കുക (take), ഇരിക്കുക (sit/stay), നോക്കുക (see). Memorise these and you can order food, find toilets, make friends and survive beautifully.

The miracle: verbs don't conjugate by person. ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (I go), നീ പോകുന്നു (you go), അവൻ പോകുന്നു (he goes), അവർ പോകുന്നു (they go) — one form fits all. Learn tense once, use it for everyone: പോയി (went), പോകും (will go).

Polite commands end in -ൂ: പോകൂ (please go), വരൂ (please come), കഴിക്കൂ (please eat), പറയൂ (please say). This one ending turns every order into an invitation — it is the most useful suffix in Malayalam, worth more than a hundred nouns.

Existence closes the kit: ഉണ്ട് (und — it is / there is) anchors locations — പുസ്തകം മേശമേൽ ഉണ്ട് (the book is on the table). ഇല്ല (illa — there isn't) removes — പണം ഇല്ല (no money). Twelve verbs plus ഉണ്ട്/ഇല്ല: the engine room of Malayalam.

topics.desc: Water, money, time, today — the everyday Malayalam words that unlock daily life. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Time words first: ഇന്ന് (today), നാളെ (tomorrow), ഇന്നലെ (yesterday), ഇപ്പോൾ (now). You will use them ten times a day — shopping, planning, chatting — while rare nouns gather dust.
faqs.q: Which words pay off fastest?

faqs.a: Malayalam happily absorbs English — ബസ് (bus), ടിക്കറ്റ് (ticket), ഓഫീസ് (office). Use the pure Malayalam word when you know it, the loanword when you don't. Fluency first, purity later.
faqs.q: Is mixing English okay?

faqs.a: Nouns first, verbs second, adjectives third. With fifty nouns and the twelve verbs from the verbs page, you can point, ask and survive — grammar glues them later.
faqs.q: Nouns or verbs first?

topics.note: A note on ഇന്ന്, നാളെ, ഇന്നലെ. Malayalam time words pivot around today: ഇന്ന് (inn — today), നാളെ (naale — tomorrow), ഇന്നലെ (innale — yesterday). Master this trio and half your daily sentences assemble themselves — നാളെ കാണാം (see you tomorrow) alone is worth the lesson.
paras: Survival runs on nouns: വെള്ളം (vellam — water), ആഹാരം (aahaaram — food), വീട് (veed — home), പണം (panam — money), സമയം (samayam — time). Five words, and you can ask for water, find home, handle money and ask the time — the entire first day in a new city.

Movement words come next: റോഡ് (road — road), ബസ് (bus — bus), കട (kada — shop), സ്കൂൾ (school — school). Kerala moves by bus and foot; knowing ബസ് സ്റ്റാന്റ് എവിടെ? (where is the bus stand?) saves more time than any app.

Opinions need adjectives: നല്ല (nalla — good), വലിയ (valiya — big), ചെറിയ (cheriya — small), പുതിയ (puthiya — new), പഴയ (pazhaya — old). നല്ലത് (nallath — that's good) approves everything from food to plans — the most useful single opinion in Malayalam.

Weather and mood close the kit: മഴ (mazha — rain) matters half the year, വെയിൽ (veyil — sun/heat) the other half. മഴ പെയ്യുന്നു (rain is coming) starts conversations with strangers; in Kerala, weather talk is friendship's front door.

faqs.a: Point and say ഇത് ഒന്ന് (ith onn — one of these) — it works in every chayakada, mess and bakery in Kerala. Add ദയവായി (please) and a smile; grammar can wait until dessert.
faqs.q: How do I order with almost no Malayalam?

faqs.a: എരിവ് കുറച്ച് (eriv kurach — less spicy, please). Kerala food honours chilli and coconut deeply; this one sentence saves sensitive stomachs while keeping every flavour.
faqs.q: How do I ask for less spicy food?

faqs.a: രുചിയുണ്ട് (ruchiyund — it's delicious). Say it to the cook, the server, the ammama who packed your lunch — it is the highest compliment in Malayali food culture.

topics.note: A note on സദ്യ. The Onam sadya — rice, sambar, avial, thoran, pachadi, payasam on a banana leaf — is Kerala on a plate. Eat with the right hand, start from the left, finish with payasam, and understand the state in one feast.
paras: Breakfast is the glory: അപ്പം (appam — lacy hoppers), പുട്ട് (puttu — steamed cylinders), ഇഡ്ഡലി (iddali — steamed cakes), ദോശ (dosha — crisp crepe), all served with സാമ്പാർ (saambaar) and ചമ്മന്തി (chammanthi — coconut chutney). ചായ കുടിച്ചോ? (have you had tea?) is asked with love — answer honestly, then accept seconds.

Meals centre on ഊണ് (oon — the rice meal): ചോറ് (chor — rice), സാമ്പാർ, രസം (rasam — pepper-tamarind soup), മീൻ കറി (meen kari — fish curry), തൈര് (thayir — curd), പപ്പടം (pappadam — crisp papad). Served on banana leaves at weddings, eaten with the right hand — ഊണ് റെഡിയാണോ? (is the meal ready?) is the happiest question.

Taste words steer every order: എരിവ് (eriv — spicy), മധുരം (madhuram — sweet), പുളി (puli — sour), ഉപ്പ് (upp — salt). കുറച്ച് ഉപ്പ് (a little salt), പഞ്ചസാര വേണ്ട (no sugar) — with taste words, your plate obeys you.

Drinks and bills close the meal: കാപ്പി (coffee), ചായ (tea — the famous bed-tea!), മോര് (mor — buttermilk), പഴച്ചാറ് (pazhachaar — juice). ബില്ല് തരൂ (please give the bill) ends it; രുചിയുണ്ടായിരുന്നു (it was delicious) guarantees a smile on your way out.

topics.desc: ഴ, റ-ര, ള — every tricky Malayalam sound, one by one, with examples. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ര is a light flap (like the dd in American cuter); റ is a hard trill (rolled r). മരം (maram — tree) versus കറുത്ത (karutha — black). Practise pairs daily until your tongue files them separately.
faqs.q: What is the difference between ര and റ?

faqs.a: ള is retroflex — tongue curled back: പള്ളി (school), വെള്ളം (water). ല is dental — tongue on teeth. Say la-la sliding tongue back and feel the shift.
faqs.q: How do I make the ള sound?

faqs.a: Curl the tongue back toward the roof WITHOUT touching, and voice it — between r, l and a French j. പഴം, വാഴ, മഴ. Children take years to perfect it, so forgive yourself months — then enjoy the applause.
faqs.q: How do I pronounce ഴ?

topics.note: A note on ഴ (zha). Malayalam's signature sound, shared with Tamil: curl the tongue back WITHOUT touching the roof, and voice it — പഴം (fruit), വാഴ (plantain), മഴ (rain). Three everyday words, one legendary sound. Master ഴ and Kerala applauds.
paras: The two r's split soft and hard: ര is a single flap — മരം (maram — tree), വലിയ (valiya — big) — while റ trills hard — കറുത്ത (karutha — black). English ears merge them; Malayalam meaning doesn't. Practise pairs daily until your tongue files them separately.
The liquid ള curls back: പള്ളി (palli — school), വെള്ളം (vellam — water). Contrast ല (dental, tongue on teeth) with ള (retroflex, curled). Glide la-lla daily; the roof-touch becomes reflex.

Dental versus retroflex stops: ത (teeth — തല, head) against ട (roof — കോട്ട, fort). Hold a finger to your lips: dentals puff forward, retroflexes pop upward. Ten minutes of ത-ട alternation retunes the mouth within a week.

The rest behave kindly: ച is cha at word start (ചായ) softening inside words, ണ marks retroflex n (കണ്ണ് — eye), and long vowels simply hold double — ആ, ഈ, ഊ. Malayalam spelling mirrors speech faithfully: pronounce what you see, and you are right nine times in ten.

topics.desc: Verb last, respect built in — Malayalam grammar in plain English, no jargon walls. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Put the verb last: ഞാൻ പുസ്തകം വായിക്കുന്നു (I book read). Subject-Object-Verb, always. English instincts will fight you for a week; then SOV feels like home.
faqs.q: Where does the verb go?

faqs.a: എനിക്ക് (enikk — to me), നിനക്ക് (ninakk — to you familiar), നിങ്ങൾക്ക് (ningalkk — to you formal). എനിക്ക് വെള്ളം വേണം (I want water) is literally to-me water is-wanted — Malayalam wants flow toward people.
faqs.q: How do I say I want something?

faqs.a: ഇത് (ith — this, near me), അത് (ath — that, far). ഇത് എന്താണ്? (what is this?) points at anything within reach; mastery takes one shopping trip.
faqs.q: How do this and that work?

topics.note: A note on -ന് / -ക്ക്. Malayalam's dative ending aims verbs at people and places: എനിക്ക് (to me), സ്കൂളിലേക്ക് (to school), വീട്ടിലേക്ക് (homeward). Sentences like എനിക്ക് മനസ്സിലായി (to-me it-is-understood = I understand) reveal Malayalam's worldview: experiences come TO you.
paras: Malayalam sentences end with the verb: ഞാൻ പുസ്തകം വായിക്കുന്നു (I — book — read). Subject first, object middle, verb last — SOV, the order of half the world's languages. Rearrange your English instincts once, and every Malayalam sentence parses cleanly.

Small endings do heavy work: -ഇൽ (il — in/on) places things — വീട്ടിൽ (at home), മേശമേൽ (on the table); -ഓട് (od — with) joins company — സുഹൃത്തിനോട് (with a friend); -ക്ക് (kk) aims motion and wanting — സ്കൂളിലേക്ക് (to school), എനിക്ക് വേണം (I want). Endings, not word order, carry Malayalam meaning.

Questions rise at the end: നിങ്ങൾ എവിടെ പോകുന്നു? (where are you going?) — എവിടെ (where), എന്ത് (what), ആര് (who), എന്തിന് (why), എങ്ങനെ (how), എപ്പോൾ (when). Yes-no questions add -ഓ (-o): ഭക്ഷണം കഴിച്ചോ? (have you eaten?). Question words plus rising tone — asking is easy.

Negation stays simple: ഇല്ല (illa) denies existence — പണം ഇല്ല (no money); verb forms deny actions — എനിക്ക് അറിയില്ല (I don't know); വേണ്ട (venda) refuses — പഞ്ചസാര വേണ്ട (no sugar, thanks). Three no's for three jobs — Malayalam refuses precisely.

faqs.q: What are the first five words?

faqs.a: Fifteen focused minutes beat two distracted hours. One topic page, every speaker tapped, five words reviewed — daily beats heroic.
faqs.q: How much should I study daily?

faqs.a: No — speak first, script second. Roman letters carry you through months of conversation; the alphabet page waits patiently until curiosity pulls you in.

topics.note: A note on അതെ, ശരി and ആ. Malayalam yes comes in three flavours: അതെ (athe — respectful yes), ശരി (shari — okay/agreed), ആ (aa — casual yeah). Learners live on അതെ and ശരി — respectful, warm, never wrong. Save ആ for friends.
paras: Week one needs eleven words: നമസ്കാരം (hello), അതെ (yes), ശരി (okay), നന്ദി (thanks), ദയവായി (please), ഞാൻ (I), നിങ്ങൾ (you, formal), ഇത് എന്താണ്? (what is this?), മനസ്സിലായി (I understand), അറിയില്ല (I don't know), പോകാം (let's go). Eleven words, and you can greet, agree, thank, ask, confess ignorance and move — the whole beginner game.

Pronouns branch early: ഞാൻ (I), നിങ്ങൾ (you formal/plural), നീ (you familiar), അവൻ/അവൾ (he/she), അവർ (they formal), ഞങ്ങൾ (we exclusive), നമ്മൾ (we inclusive). Two we's where English has one — നമ്മൾ പോകാം (let's go, you included) is Malayalam's warmest invitation.

Quantity words multiply everything: കുറച്ച് (a little), ഒരുപാട് (a lot), മതി (enough), മാത്രം (only). കുറച്ച് മലയാളം സംസാരിക്കും (I speak a little Malayalam) is the perfect learner's confession — humble, charming, instantly rewarded with help.

Action invitations close week one: ഇവിടെ വരൂ (come here), ഇരിക്കൂ (please sit), കഴിക്കൂ (please eat), പോകാം (let's go). These four run hospitality, the beating heart of Malayali culture — learn them and you stop being a guest and start being family.

topics.desc: അമ്മ, അച്ഛൻ, ചേട്ടൻ, ചേച്ചി — family words, including the elder-younger split. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Yes — Malayalam splits siblings by age: ചേട്ടൻ (elder brother) versus അനിയൻ (younger brother), ചേച്ചി (elder sister) versus അനിയത്തി (younger sister). Age order is grammar in Malayali families.
faqs.q: Why two words for brother?

faqs.a: ചേട്ടൻ (chettan) and ചേച്ചി (chechi) address any slightly-older man or woman — shopkeepers, colleagues, strangers. It borrows family warmth for the whole world.
faqs.q: Can I call strangers chettan and chechi?

faqs.a: നിങ്ങളുടെ കുടുംബത്തിൽ എത്ര പേർ? (how many people in your family?) — then listen proudly to the answer. Family questions are love in Malayali culture.
faqs.q: How do I ask about family?

topics.lede: അമ്മ, അച്ഛൻ, ചേട്ടൻ, ചേച്ചി — family, including the elder-younger split.
topics.note: A note on അമ്മാവൻ, അമ്മായി. Malayali kinship runs precise: അമ്മാവൻ (mother's brother / respected uncle), അമ്മായി (auntie), ചേട്ടത്തി (elder brother's wife). Learners need the big six first; the full map unfolds at weddings.
paras: Parents anchor everything: അമ്മ (amma — mother) and അച്ഛൻ (achchhan — father) — the first words of every Malayali child and the warmest words in the language. അമ്മ calls across market crowds; അച്ഛൻ advises over evening chaya. Learn them with love, not just memory.

Siblings split by age, never blend: ചേട്ടൻ (elder brother), അനിയൻ (younger brother), ചേച്ചി (elder sister), അനിയത്തി (younger sister). There is no plain brother — every brother is elder or younger, and the word you choose declares the hierarchy. Ask ages early; address correctly always.

Grandparents rule the roost: മുത്തച്ഛൻ (muttachchhan — grandfather) and മുത്തശ്ശി (muttashshi — grandmother) — storytellers, sweet-sneakers, family courts of final appeal. മുത്തശ്ശി കഥ (grandmother's tale) is a whole genre; മുത്തച്ഛൻ advice ends arguments. Respect flows upward; treats flow down.

The wider net holds daily life: അമ്മാവൻ (uncle), അമ്മായി (auntie), ഭർത്താവ് (husband), ഭാര്യ (wife), കുടുംബം (family itself). എന്റെ കുടുംബം (my family) introduces them all — practise the sentence with your own names filled in, because you will say it at every Malayali gathering forever.

topics.desc: Seven days, four day-parts, weeks and months — Malayalam time from morning to month. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Start the week Sunday like Malayalam calendars: ഞായർ, തിങ്കൾ, ചൊവ്വ, ബുധൻ, വ്യാഴം, വെള്ളി, ശനി. Chant them in order — rhythm makes them permanent.
faqs.q: How do I memorise the days?

faqs.a: രാവിലെ (morning), ഉച്ച (afternoon), വൈകുന്നേരം (evening), രാത്രി (night). Greetings, meals and plans all key off these four — ശുഭസായാഹ്നം (good evening) after four-ish.
faqs.q: How does Malayalam split the day?

faqs.a: ആഴ്ച (aazhcha — week), മാസം (maasam — month), വർഷം (varsham — year). അടുത്ത ആഴ്ച (next week), ഈ മാസം (this month) — plans assemble instantly.
faqs.q: Week, month, year?

topics.note: A note on വെള്ളി and ചൊവ്വ. Friday (വെള്ളി) and Tuesday (ചൊവ്വ) are auspicious days — temples fill, new ventures launch, ദേവി worship peaks. Knowing the days means knowing the rhythm: never schedule a sceptical meeting on a festival Friday.
paras: The week runs Sunday-first: ഞായർ (Sunday), തിങ്കൾ (Monday), ചൊവ്വ (Tuesday), ബുധൻ (Wednesday), വ്യാഴം (Thursday), വെള്ളി (Friday), ശനി (Saturday). Planet-named like most of Asia — the sky keeps Malayalam's calendar.

Day-parts steer greetings and meals: രാവിലെ (morning — സുപ്രഭാതം), ഉച്ച (afternoon — lunch/oon o'clock), വൈകുന്നേരം (evening — chaya round two), രാത്രി (night — goodnight is usually just നമസ്കാരം with a smile).

Bigger units plan life: ആഴ്ച (week), മാസം (month), വർഷം (year) — അടുത്ത ആഴ്ച (next week), കഴിഞ്ഞ മാസം (last month), ഈ വർഷം (this year). Malayalam plans in weeks for errands, months for visits, years for weddings.

Dates assemble simply: തീയതി (theeyathi — date), ഒന്നാം തീയതി (first), ഇന്ന് തീയതി എത്ര? (what's today's date?). Numbers from the numbers page slot straight in — പതിനഞ്ചാം തീയതി (the 15th). Time, dates, plans: one page, total coverage.

topics.desc: Stations, directions, tickets and toilets — travel Malayalam that gets you there. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ...എവിടെ? (...evide — where is...?) plus a pointing finger. ബസ് സ്റ്റാന്റ് എവിടെ? റെയിൽവേ സ്റ്റേഷൻ എവിടെ? One pattern, every destination in Kerala.
faqs.q: How do I ask where things are?

faqs.a: ഇടത് (left), വലത് (right), നേരെ (straight) — then അടുത്ത് (near) and ദൂരെ (far). Malayalam directions come with generous hand-waving; watch the hands as well as the words.
faqs.q: Left, right, straight?

faqs.a: ടോയ്ലറ്റ് എവിടെ? (where is the toilet?) — say it clearly, without embarrassment. Every bus stand, station and restaurant understands instantly.
faqs.q: How do I find a toilet?

topics.note: A note on സ്റ്റേഷൻ. സ്റ്റേഷൻ (station) anchors every journey: ബസ് സ്റ്റാന്റ് (bus stand), റെയിൽവേ സ്റ്റേഷൻ (railway station), വിമാനത്താവളം (airport). Learn the pattern once — vehicle + സ്റ്റേഷൻ — and every signboard in Kerala reads itself.
paras: Destinations unlock with one pattern: ബസ് സ്റ്റാന്റ് (bus stand), റെയിൽവേ സ്റ്റേഷൻ (railway station), വിമാനത്താവളം (airport), ഹോട്ടൽ (hotel). Add എവിടെ? (where?) and you can find every transport hub in the state — സ്റ്റേഷൻ എവിടെ? is the traveller's master key.

Directions come in threes: ഇടത് (left), വലത് (right), നേരെ (straight ahead) — plus അടുത്ത് (nearby) and ദൂരെ (far). ഇടതുവശത്ത് (on the left side), നേരെ പോകൂ (go straight) — follow the words, watch the inevitable hand gestures, arrive smiling.

Tickets and seats run the journey: ടിക്കറ്റ് (ticket), ഒരു ടിക്കറ്റ് (one ticket), എത്ര? (how much?), സീറ്റ് (seat). ബസ് എപ്പോൾ വരും? (when does the bus come?) — asked at every stand, answered with cheerful vagueness. Patience is also vocabulary.

Emergencies and essentials close the kit: സഹായം (help), ടോയ്ലറ്റ് എവിടെ? (where is the toilet?), വെള്ളം (water), ആശുപത്രി (hospital). Hope never to need എന്നെ സഹായിക്കൂ (please help) — but carry it always, like travel insurance in a single word.

topics.desc: Prices, bargaining and colours — shop in Malayalam from first price to final deal. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: വില എത്ര? (what's the price?) — then എത്ര? (how much?) for everything else. Two questions, every shop in Kerala.
faqs.q: How do I ask the price?

faqs.a: വളരെ കൂടുതലാണ് (too costly) with a smile, then കുറച്ച് കുറയ്ക്കൂ (reduce a little, please). Bargaining is friendly theatre — play your part warmly and the price moves.
faqs.q: How do I bargain politely?

faqs.a: Start with five: ചുവപ്പ് (red), നീല (blue), പച്ച (green), മഞ്ഞ (yellow), വെള്ള (white). വേറെ നിറം (different colour) shows them all.
faqs.q: Which colours first?

topics.note: A note on കുറയ്ക്കൂ. കുറച്ച് കുറയ്ക്കൂ (kurach kuraykkoo — please reduce a little) is the magic sentence of Kerala markets. Said smiling, it opens every negotiation; said with വാങ്ങാം (I'll take it) right after, it closes most. Bargaining respects the dance — never the demand.
paras: Prices open every transaction: വില എത്ര? (what's the price?), എത്ര? (how much?), ഇതിന് എത്ര? (what's this one's price?). Listen for the number plus രൂപ — repeat it back to confirm — അമ്പത്? (fifty?) — and you are already shopping in Malayalam.

Bargaining follows the friendly script: വളരെ കൂടുതലാണ് (too costly), കുറച്ച് കുറയ്ക്കൂ (reduce a little), ഡിസ്കൗണ്ട് ഉണ്ടോ? (any discount?). Start walking away slowly — നന്ദി, നോക്കാം (thanks, I'll look around) — and the real price often chases you down the street.

Sizes and colours refine the hunt: വലിയത് (the bigger one), ചെറിയത് (the smaller one), പുതിയത് (a new one), വേറെ നിറം (a different colour). Point, name the change, nod — Malayali shopkeepers read gestures fluently and reward attempts instantly.

Colours close the sale: ചുവപ്പ് (red), നീല (blue), പച്ച (green), മഞ്ഞ (yellow), വെള്ള (white), കറുപ്പ് (black). ചുവപ്പ് നന്നായിരിക്കുന്നു (the red looks good) — then വാങ്ങാം (I'll take it). Deal done, in Malayalam, with a smile on both sides.

topics.desc: Help, doctor, hospital — emergency Malayalam you hope to never need. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: എന്നെ സഹായിക്കൂ (please help me) — loud, clear, repeated. Add ആശുപത്രി എവിടെ? (where is the hospital?) and Malayali crowds mobilise instantly.
faqs.q: What is the one emergency sentence?

faqs.a: Point and say ഇവിടെ വേദനിക്കുന്നു (it hurts here). Then സുഖമില്ല (I feel unwell) and ഡോക്ടറെ വേണം (I need a doctor). Pain plus pointing crosses every language gap.
faqs.q: How do I explain pain?

faqs.a: നഷ്ടപ്പെട്ടു (it is lost) — പണം നഷ്ടപ്പെട്ടു (money lost), ബാഗ് നഷ്ടപ്പെട്ടു (bag lost). Then പോലീസ് സ്റ്റേഷൻ എവിടെ? (where is the police station?).
faqs.q: How do I report something lost?

topics.lede: Help, doctor, hospital — emergency Malayalam you hope to never need.
topics.note: A note on സഹായം. സഹായം (sahaayam — help) is Malayalam's shortest lifeline — shout it and crowds come running. Kerala's bystander culture is famously kind: strangers will escort you to hospitals, translate for doctors, and refuse thanks. Ask loudly; receive gratefully.
paras: The core three save lives: സഹായം (help), അപകടം (danger), അടിയന്തരം (emergency). എന്നെ സഹായിക്കൂ (please help me) — say it to anyone, anywhere. Malayali crowds respond to distress calls faster than any app; your job is only to ask.

Medical words route the rescue: ഡോക്ടർ (doctor), ആശുപത്രി (hospital), മരുന്ന് (medicine), മെഡിക്കൽ ഷോപ്പ് (pharmacy). ആശുപത്രി എവിടെ? (where is the hospital?) plus a taxi wave — in cities, help arrives in minutes.

Symptoms speak simply: ഇവിടെ വേദനിക്കുന്നു (it hurts here — point!), സുഖമില്ല (I feel unwell), തലവേദന (headache), പനി (fever). Pain words plus pointing hands diagnose across every language barrier on earth.

Danger and loss close the kit: തീ (fire), കള്ളൻ (thief), പോലീസ് (police), നഷ്ടപ്പെട്ടു (it's lost), എംബസി (embassy). Memorise these cold — emergencies never wait for phrasebooks, and ten minutes of drilling buys total peace of mind.
topics.title: Emergency Malayalam

topics.desc: നിങ്ങൾ or നീ? വരൂ or വാ? Respect levels, decoded with examples. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: നിങ്ങൾ for every adult you don't know well — shopkeepers, officials, elders, strangers. നീ waits for close friends, children and family. Wrong-side errors embarrass; learners are forgiven, but respect first is always safest.
faqs.q: When do I use നിങ്ങൾ?

faqs.a: Add -ൂ: വാ becomes വരൂ, പോ becomes പോകൂ, പറ becomes പറയൂ. One ending, instant politeness — the highest-value suffix in Malayalam.
faqs.q: How do I make a command polite?

faqs.a: സാർ (saar — sir) and ചേച്ചി/ചേട്ടൻ for slightly-older strangers. സാർ, സമയം എത്ര? (sir, what time is it?). Better than pointing and shouting in any language.
faqs.q: How do I address strangers?

topics.lede: നിങ്ങൾ or നീ? വരൂ or വാ? Respect levels, decoded.
topics.note: A note on -ൂ. -ൂ (oo) is Malayalam's respect rocket — attach it to any verb and watch warmth ignite: വരൂ (do come), നോക്കൂ (please see), പറയൂ (please tell). One sound that upgrades every request instantly.
paras: Malayalam has two yous: നിങ്ങൾ (formal/plural — strangers, elders, officials) and നീ (familiar — friends, children, family). English erased this distinction centuries ago; Malayalam keeps it razor-sharp. Every conversation opens with an invisible choice — make it consciously, and make it respectful.

Verbs mirror the split: വരൂ (please come) versus വാ (come!), പറയൂ (please say) versus പറ (say!), പോകൂ (please go) versus പോ (go!). The -ൂ ending is pure respect — same verb, different universe. Stem-alone orders bark; -ൂ invites.

Giving and forgiving show the range: തരൂ (please give) versus താ (give!), ക്ഷമിക്കണം (please forgive) versus ക്ഷമിക്ക് (forgive, familiar). Beggars and kings both hear തരൂ — politeness in Malayalam costs nothing and buys everything.

Strangers get titles: സാർ (sir), ചേട്ടൻ (brother), ചേച്ചി (sister). സാർ, സഹായിക്കൂ (sir, please help) opens any door; barking orders at strangers closes them. Malayali warmth is earned with two syllables of respect.
topics.title: Formal and informal Malayalam

topics.desc: Verb-first sentences, ഞാൻ വേണം, ഇല്ല vs അല്ല — fix the classic errors. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: English order with Malayalam words: ഞാൻ പോ instead of ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു, verb first, question words misplaced. Cure: every sentence ends with the verb — practise SOV until English order feels foreign.
faqs.q: What is the most common mistake?

faqs.a: Wanting flows toward people: എനിക്ക് വേണം (to-me it-is-wanted), never ഞാൻ വേണം. One of Malayalam's deepest patterns — experiences come TO you — and beginners fight it for weeks.
faqs.q: Why is ഞാൻ വേണം wrong?

faqs.a: ഇല്ല denies existence and possession — പണം ഇല്ല (no money); അല്ല denies identity — ഞാൻ വിദ്യാർത്ഥി അല്ല (I am not a student). Two no's, two jobs, zero overlap.
faqs.q: ഇല്ല or അല്ല?

topics.lede: Verb-first sentences, ഞാൻ വേണം, ഇല്ല vs അല്ല — fix them all.
topics.note: A note on തെറ്റ്. തെറ്റ് (thett — mistake) is the kindest word in this lesson — എന്റെ തെറ്റ് (my mistake) disarms every situation. Malayalis adore learners who err boldly and laugh warmly; the only true തെറ്റ് is silence.
paras: Mistake one: English word order. ഞാൻ പോ (I go — bare stem, wrong) instead of ഞാൻ പോകുന്നു (I go — conjugated, right); verbs wandering mid-sentence instead of anchoring the end. Malayalam is verb-final, always — SOV is not a suggestion, it is the law.

Mistake two: ഞാൻ വേണം (I want — wrong) instead of എനിക്ക് വേണം (to-me wanted — right). Malayalam wanting flows toward the wanter; English wanting fires from the wanter. Flip the arrow and dozens of sentences — എനിക്ക് മനസ്സിലായി, എനിക്കറിയാം — unlock at once.

Mistake three: one-size no. ഇല്ല denies existence — പണം ഇല്ല (there's no money); അല്ല denies identity — ഞാൻ ടീച്ചർ അല്ല (I am not a teacher). Beginners spray ഇല്ല everywhere; natives smile and correct. Learn both no's, use each precisely.

Mistake four: rushing sounds — flat long vowels, merged r's, skipped -ൂ. പതുക്കെ (slowly), ശരിയായി (correctly), വീണ്ടും (again): the holy trinity of repair. ശ്രമം (effort) plus പരിശീലനം (practice) plus ക്ഷമ (patience) — and അഭിനന്ദനങ്ങൾ, mistakes become fluency.

topics.desc: Stop translating in your head — shadowing, thinking aloud and brave first speeches. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Shadow natives: play a Malayalam sentence, repeat it aloud half a second behind, matching rhythm and melody. Ten minutes daily rewires your mouth faster than any textbook.
faqs.q: What is the fastest speaking drill?

faqs.a: Yes — narrate your day in Malayalam: ഞാൻ ചായ കുടിക്കുന്നു (I'm drinking tea), ഞാൻ സ്കൂളിൽ പോകുന്നു. Thinking aloud turns dead time into speaking practice.
faqs.q: Should I talk to myself in Malayalam?

faqs.a: Perfectionism. Malayalis reward every attempt and correct with love — സംസാരിക്കൂ, തെറ്റ് കുഴപ്പമില്ല (speak, mistakes are fine). Fluency is corrected mistakes, stacked daily.
faqs.q: What blocks speaking most?

topics.note: A note on സംസാരിക്കാം. സംസാരിക്കാം (samsaarikkaam — let's speak / we may speak) is permission and invitation in one word — വരൂ, മലയാളത്തിൽ സംസാരിക്കാം (come, let's speak in Malayalam). Say it to every patient listener; doors, hearts and vocabularies open together.
paras: Speaking starts with shadowing: play a Malayalam line, echo it half a beat behind, copying music more than words. സംഭാഷണം (conversation) is rhythm before grammar — shadow ten minutes daily and your mouth learns Malayalam's dance while your brain watches.

Questions and answers volley practice: ചോദ്യം (question) out, ഉത്തരം (answer) back. Ask yourself everything — ഇത് എന്താണ്? എവിടെ? എന്തിന്? — and answer aloud. Self-volleys feel silly for a day, then feel like fluency arriving.

Opinions and stories stretch speeches: അഭിപ്രായം (opinion), സത്യം (truth), കഥ (story). എന്റെ അഭിപ്രായം... (in my opinion...) forces full sentences; കഥ പറയൂ (tell a story) forces sequences. Opinions build sentences; stories build speakers.

Courage closes the circuit: ധൈര്യം (courage) speaks first and perfects later. പാട്ട് (songs) loosen tongues, ചിരി (laughter) dissolves fear, നിശ്ശബ്ദത (pauses) are allowed. Speak badly today — പ്രസംഗം (speech) improves only in motion.

topics.desc: Fast speech, films and radio — train your ears until Malayalam sounds slow. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Spoken Malayalam contracts: പോകുന്നു melts toward പോണു, വരുന്നു toward വരണു. Learn the full forms first, then meet the street forms — this page bridges both.
faqs.q: Why is spoken Malayalam so fast?

faqs.a: Children's films and songs first — clear speech, simple stories, endless repetition. Then റേഡിയോ dramas, then full സിനിമ (cinema). Difficulty ladders beat difficulty cliffs.
faqs.q: What should I listen to first?

faqs.a: Catch the question words — എന്ത്, എവിടെ, ആര്, എപ്പോൾ — and the verb at the end. Questions plus verbs carry eighty percent of meaning; the rest is decoration.
faqs.q: How do I catch meaning in fast speech?

topics.note: A note on മനസ്സിലായോ? മനസ്സിലായോ? (manassilaayo — do you understand?) is the kindest question in Malayalam — teachers, friends and auto drivers ask it constantly. Answer മനസ്സിലായി (understood) or കുറച്ച് കുറച്ച് (little by little); honesty tunes every speaker to your level.
paras: Listening begins with attention: ശ്രദ്ധ (attention) — ശ്രദ്ധിച്ച് കേൾക്കൂ (listen carefully). Malayalam sentences save the verb for last, so ears must hold the whole sentence before meaning lands. Patience is a listening skill; practise holding, not guessing.

Street Malayalam contracts beautifully: പോകുന്നു → പോണു, വരുന്നു → വരണു. Textbooks teach the full forms; ears must learn the melted ones. Listen for the verb-ghost at sentence end — the meaning hides there.

Media ladders the difficulty: പാട്ട് (songs) first — slow, repetitive, emotional; വാർത്തകൾ (news) next — clear, formal, standard; റേഡിയോ (radio) drama third — fast, natural, fun; സിനിമ (films) last — slang, speed, glory. Climb rung by rung; never leap.

Active listening closes the loop: വീണ്ടും കേൾക്കൂ (listen again), ധ്വനി (sound) by ധ്വനി. Replay each line three times — once for music, once for words, once for meaning. Three passes per line, ten lines per day: ears transform within a month.

topics.desc: Words to sentences to stories — reading Malayalam from first signs to full pages. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Signboards: കട (shop), സ്റ്റേഷൻ (station), ഹോട്ടൽ (restaurant) — big letters, daily repetition, instant rewards. Streets teach faster than textbooks.
faqs.q: What should I read first?

faqs.a: Children's books — short വാക്യം (sentences), pictures for context, full conjuncts. Then comics, then പത്രം headlines, then articles.
faqs.q: When am I ready for books?

faqs.a: Keep a നിഘണ്ടു (dictionary) app open and mine unknown words — five per page, no more. Reading with a dictionary beats studying word lists: context glues memory.
faqs.q: How do I handle unknown words?

topics.lede: Words to sentences to stories — reading from first signs to full pages.
topics.note: A note on പത്രം. Malayalam newspapers — മലയാള മനോരമ, മാതൃഭൂമി — use formal written Malayalam, nobler than street speech. Headlines first: big type, short lines, daily habit. One headline a day keeps illiteracy away.
paras: Reading starts with words: വാക്ക് (word) by വാക്ക് — വായിക്കൂ (please read) signs, labels, names. Malayalam spelling mirrors speech, so sounding out works: see കട, say kada, know shop. Phonetic scripts reward beginners richly.

Sentences assemble next: വാക്യം (sentence) — subject, object, verb-last. Read SOV sentences end-first for meaning: find the verb, then ask who-did-what. Backwards parsing feels odd for a week, then automatic forever.

Paragraphs and articles follow: ഖണ്ഡിക (paragraph), ലേഖനം (article), കവിത (poem). Children's stories first — short, illustrated, kind — then മാസിക (magazines), then സാഹിത്യം (literature) itself. Malayalam's written heritage spans a thousand years; start at the shallow end.

Dictionaries deepen everything: നിഘണ്ടു (dictionary) — five new words per page, written down, reviewed nightly. Reading without recording entertains; reading with recording teaches. Mine every page; keep every gem.
topics.title: Reading Malayalam

topics.desc: Letters to lists to letters — writing Malayalam from first strokes to full pages. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Round strokes before all: Malayalam letters flow circular — അ, ആ, ഉ, എ — so practise circles and hooks first. Trace big, shrink slowly; കൈയെഴുത്ത് (handwriting) beautifies with mileage.
faqs.q: How do I start writing Malayalam?

faqs.a: പട്ടിക (lists): shopping lists, word lists, daily plans. Lists forgive grammar, demand spelling, and get used — the perfect beginner writing.
faqs.q: What should I write first?

faqs.a: കത്ത് (letters) to friends, കുറിപ്പ് (notes) to self, വീട്ടുപാഠം (homework) for courses. Real writing to real readers beats copied exercises every time.
faqs.q: When real writing?

topics.lede: Letters to lists to letters — writing from first strokes to full pages.
topics.note: A note on ഒപ്പ്. Your ഒപ്പ് (signature) in Malayalam script is a milestone — practise it until it flows in one confident motion. Signing Malayalam-style on forms, cards and letters declares belonging more than any certificate.
paras: Writing starts with strokes: Malayalam letters curve and loop — എഴുതൂ (please write) circles, hooks and waves before full letters. Trace അ ആ ഇ ഈ ഉ ഊ big and slow; the hand learns shapes the eye already knows.
Tools matter little, mileage matters all: പേന (pen), pencil, finger on steamed mirrors — Malayali children trace in rice, sand and air. Write everywhere; medium is vanity, motion is learning.

Lists graduate the hand: പട്ടിക (list) — കുറിപ്പ് (notes), വിലാസം (addresses), തീയതി (dates). Copy your own പേര് (name) fifty times, then friends' names, then street names. Familiar words, fresh script: the fastest fluent hand.

Real writing arrives: കത്ത് (letters), അപേക്ഷ (applications), പരീക്ഷ (exams), വീട്ടുപാഠം (homework). Write a postcard to yourself in Malayalam — short, joyful, posted. First posted Malayalam is never forgotten.
topics.title: Writing Malayalam

topics.desc: Who does what, verb last — Malayalam sentences decoded with living examples. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Subject-Object-Verb: ഞാൻ പുസ്തകം വായിക്കുന്നു (I book read). Endings mark roles, so order flexes for emphasis — but verb-last is home.
faqs.q: What is Malayalam word order?

faqs.a: Tense lives on the verb, same for all persons: പോകുന്നു (go-present), പോയി (went), പോകും (will go). Time words — ഇന്നലെ, ഇന്ന്, നാളെ — frame it; the verb carries it.
faqs.q: How do tenses work?

faqs.a: Add -ഓ and rise: അത് നിന്റെ പുസ്തകമാണോ? (is that your book?). Question words — എന്ത്, എവിടെ, ആര് — sit where the answer would.
faqs.q: How do I ask questions?

topics.lede: Who does what, verb last — sentences decoded with living examples.
topics.note: A note on മഴ പെയ്യുന്നു. Malayalam weather does things: മഴ പെയ്യുന്നു (rain rains), വെയിൽ അടിക്കുന്നു (sun strikes), കാറ്റ് വീശുന്നു (wind blows). No empty it — Malayalam skies act. Weather sentences teach SOV with zero confusion: subject, then verb, done.
paras: Simple sentences stack three blocks: ഞാൻ സ്കൂളിൽ പോകുന്നു (I — to-school — go), അവൾ പാട്ട് പാടുന്നു (she — song — sings), ഞങ്ങൾ മലയാളം പഠിക്കുന്നു (we — Malayalam — study). Subject, object, verb — build a hundred of these and Malayalam skeleton is yours.

Animals make perfect practice: ആൺകുട്ടി ചിരിക്കുന്നു (the boy laughs), നായ് കുരയ്ക്കുന്നു (the dog barks), പൂച്ച ഉറങ്ങുന്നു (the cat sleeps). Short subjects, vivid verbs, zero ambiguity — describe every creature you meet and SOV becomes reflex.

Time flexes the frame: ഞാൻ നാളെ വരും (I'll come tomorrow), ഇന്നലെ മഴ പെയ്തു (it rained yesterday). Time words float — front for emphasis, middle for flow — while the verb holds the end. Tense plus time word: past, present, future, mastered.

Identity and questions close the set: ഇത് എന്റെ വീടാണ് (this is my house), അത് നിന്റെ പുസ്തകമാണോ? (is that your book?), എല്ലാം ശരിയാണ് (all is well). Equate with ഇത്/അത്, question with -ഓ, reassure with എല്ലാം ശരിയാണ് — sentences for every situation.

topics.desc: Rahul becomes രാഹുൽ — spell, write and own your name in Malayalam script. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Sound it out in Malayalam letters: Rahul → രാഹുൽ, Priya → പ്രിയ, John → ജോൺ. Malayalam spells by ear — say your name slowly, catch each sound, write each letter.
faqs.q: How do I write my name in Malayalam?

faqs.a: Loan letters — ജ (ja), ഹ (ha), ശ ഷ സ (sha/sa), ഫ (fa) — handle foreign sounds. ജോൺ (John), ഫോൺ (phone) — borrowed letters for borrowed names, fully Malayalam now.
faqs.q: What about sounds Malayalam lacks?

faqs.a: ആദ്യത്തെ അക്ഷരം (first letter) starts it, അവസാനത്തെ അക്ഷരം (last letter) ends it. Introduce with എന്റെ പേര്... (my name is...), then write it — introductions stick twice as well written.
faqs.q: How do I introduce my name?

topics.lede: Rahul becomes രാഹുൽ — spell, write and own your name in Malayalam.
topics.note: A note on രാഹുൽ. Foreign names glide in Malayalam script — Rahul appears as രാഹുൽ with a soft ഹ, sometimes റാഹുൽ with a trill. All are read Rahul; none is wrong. Malayalam welcomes foreign names with flexible spelling — pick the shape you love and own it.
paras: Names transliterate by ear: break yours into sounds, match each to Malayalam letters — രവി (Ravi), ലക്ഷ്മി (Lakshmi), കിരൺ (Kiran) show the pattern. Say it slow, write it true — സ്പെല്ലിംഗ് (spelling) by sound, not by English letters.
Foreign sounds borrow loan letters: ജ for John (ജോൺ), ഫ for phones (ഫോൺ), ശ for Sharma sounds. These Sanskrit-born letters are Malayalam citizens now — use them proudly for every imported sound.

Introductions pair speech and script: പരിചയം (introduction) — എന്റെ പേര്... (my name is...), spoken, then written. പേര് ബോർഡുകൾ (name boards) on doors and desks teach daily — read every board, collect every name.

Nicknames warm everything: വിളിപ്പേര് (nickname) — മുത്ത് (pearl/darling), മോന് (son/dear), മോള് (daughter/dear). Malayalam shortens with love: Ravi becomes രവി, Lakshmi becomes ലച്ചു. Earn a Malayalam nickname and you have arrived.
topics.title: Write your name in Malayalam

topics.desc: അടിപൊളി, മച്ചാൻ, വേറെ ലെവൽ — street Malayalam that films, friends and fun run on. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: സൂപ്പർ (super) and അടിപൊളി (awesome) — positive, universal, safe. Sprinkle them on food, films and friends; instant insider status.
faqs.q: What slang is safe everywhere?

faqs.a: മച്ചാൻ (dude) and അളിയാ (bro) — for friends only, never elders or strangers. Friendship slang misused offends; rightly used, it bonds instantly.
faqs.q: Can I call people machchaan?

faqs.a: വെറുതെ (just like that / for fun) — വെറുതെ പറഞ്ഞതാണ് (just kidding), വെറുതെ വന്നതാണ് (just dropped by). The most Malayalam word in existence: purposeless joy, declared proudly.
faqs.q: What does veruthe mean?

topics.lede: അടിപൊളി, മച്ചാൻ, വേറെ ലെവൽ — street Malayalam that fun runs on.
topics.note: A note on വെറുതെ. വെറുതെ (veruthe) defies translation — just because, for fun, no reason, chill. എന്തിന്? — വെറുതെ (why? — just because). Whole philosophies hide in three syllables; use it freely, smile always.
paras: Praise slang opens doors: സൂപ്പർ (super), അടിപൊളി (awesome), വേറെ ലെവൽ (next level), കിടിലം (rocking), അയ്യടാ (wow). Food, films, friends' outfits — praise everything loudly. Malayalis praise generously; learners should too.

Friendship words bond crews: മച്ചാൻ (dude), അളിയാ (bro), ബ്രോ (bro) — friends-only, always warm. മച്ചാനേ വാടാ (come on dude) starts a thousand conversations daily. Never aim them upward at elders; sideways at friends, fire freely.

Reaction words colour stories: അയ്യോ (oh no!), അയ്യടാ (wow!), കഥ പറയാതെ (stop making things up!). Malayali storytelling runs on reactions — gasp, laugh, disbelieve theatrically. Flat faces kill stories; big reactions feed them.

Playful edges season everything: പോടാ (get lost — playful among friends, rude otherwise), ഛെ (mild disgust), വെറുതെ (just because). Learn the edges, respect the edges: slang's power is knowing exactly where fun ends.
topics.title: Malayalam slang

topics.desc: Toys, moons, stars and good-child gold — Malayalam for little learners, big joy. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Songs and കഥ (stories) — പാട്ട് with actions, tales with voices. Children absorb Malayalam through music and play long before grammar.
faqs.q: How do kids learn Malayalam best?

faqs.a: നല്ല കുട്ടി (good child) — praise every attempt loudly. Malayali parenting runs on encouragement; learners of all ages bloom under it.
faqs.q: How do I praise a child?

faqs.a: കളി (games): name objects — പന്ത്! കളിപ്പാട്ടം! — count steps, sing counts. Play first, words hitchhike.
faqs.q: Games or lessons?

topics.lede: Toys, moons, stars and gold stars — Malayalam for little learners, big joy.
topics.note: A note on മുത്ത്. മുത്ത് (muthth — pearl/darling) melts every Malayali heart — എന്റെ മുത്ത് (my darling) for children, pets and beloveds. Terms of endearment are Malayalam's mother tongue; every child swims in them.
paras: Little learners start with love: കുട്ടികൾ (children), കുഞ്ഞ് (baby), മുത്ത് (darling), നല്ല കുട്ടി (good child). Malayali childhood floats on affection-words — call every child മുത്ത് and watch faces light like ദീപാവലി.
Play teaches fastest: കളി (play), കളിപ്പാട്ടം (toy), പന്ത് (ball) — കളിക്കാം (let's play)! Count throws, name colours, chase and giggle. Play first; Malayalam hitchhikes on joy.
School words structure days: സ്കൂൾ (school), ടീച്ചർ (teacher), പാഠം (lesson), വീട്ടുപാഠം (homework). നമസ്കാരം ടീച്ചർ (hello teacher) opens every school day — respect and learning, hand in hand.

Sky words spark wonder: സൂര്യൻ (sun), അമ്പിളി (moon), നക്ഷത്രം (star) — അമ്പിളി നോക്ക് (look at the moon)! Night-sky Malayalam, whispered on terraces, becomes lifelong memory. Teach the sky; the child keeps the language.
